articles.title: Psychology says children can act differently around cousins than around classmates; here’s why
articles.summary: A child who talks nonstop, invents games and argues fearlessly with cousins at a family gathering may barely speak during a classroom activity.
articles.body: A child who talks nonstop, invents games and argues fearlessly with cousins at a family gathering may barely speak during a classroom activity. Another child who is confident among classmates may become possessive, competitive or unusually quiet when cousins come over. For parents, these contrasting behaviours can be puzzling. Is the child simply more comfortable with family, or does the difference reveal something about how they navigate relationships?The answer may lie in the fact that children do not experience every social setting in the same way. A cousin may be someone they have known since infancy, someone they see only during festivals, or a child they are constantly compared with by relatives. A classmate, meanwhile, belongs to a world of friendships, group dynamics, classroom rules and social expectations.Although research has not established a universal rule that children behave differently around cousins than classmates, developmental psychology offers useful insights into why their behaviour can change from one setting to another.Cousins may feel familiar, but classmates can feel like an audienceImagine a child who happily performs a dance in front of cousins during a Diwali gathering but refuses to participate when the teacher asks them to dance in front of classmates. It may be tempting to label the child shy at school and confident at home. However, confidence can depend on who is watching and how the child expects others to respond.With familiar relatives, children may already know the group's humour, habits and reactions. At school, they may be more conscious of whether their peers will laugh, approve or include them.A review published in the Journal of School Psychology, titled Childhood peer relationships: social acceptance, friendships, and peer networks, examined how children's friendships, acceptance by peers and wider social networks relate to their development and school adjustment. It highlights that relationships with peers are not all the same: having a close friend, being accepted by a group and finding one's place in a larger social network are distinct experiences.This distinction helps explain why a child might feel comfortable with one or two cousins but become withdrawn around a whole group of classmates. The difference does not automatically mean that the child lacks social skills. The social setting may simply feel more demanding.Cousins can bring out a child's playful or unfiltered sideChildren often experiment with humour, arguments, pretend play and different ways of expressing themselves when they interact with other children. How much freedom they feel to do so may depend on their relationship with the other child.A cousin who visits regularly may know a child's favourite games, recurring jokes and emotional triggers. They may have a shared history of playing together, quarrelling over toys and making up afterwards. This familiarity can make interactions feel less formal.At school, children may still be figuring out what their classmates enjoy, which jokes are acceptable and how to join a group without being left out.Research on peer relations in childhood, published in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, describes how children's peer relationships develop from the early years, with preferences for particular peers emerging in early childhood and social skills becoming more established during the preschool years.The takeaway is that children are continually learning how to relate to different people. A child who is loud and playful around cousins but measured around classmates may be responding to the different levels of familiarity and security in those relationships.However, not every cousin relationship is comfortable. Children who rarely meet their cousins, feel excluded by them or experience frequent conflict may be more guarded at family gatherings than they are with friends.Family gatherings can turn cousins into competitorsIn many Indian families, cousins are not just playmates. They may also be compared on school marks, sports, dancing, confidence or how well they behave around adults.A child who is relaxed with cousins in private may become unusually competitive when grandparents praise another child. They may interrupt conversations, refuse to share a favourite toy, boast about a school achievement or become upset when a cousin wins a game.These reactions do not necessarily mean the child dislikes their cousin. The relationship may carry an additional layer of comparison that is absent from some classroom friendships.Family comments such as “Look how neatly your cousin writes” or “Your cousin has already learnt to cycle” can make ordinary interactions feel like a competition. Even when adults intend to motivate children, repeated comparisons can influence how children view one another.Research on family relationships and children's peer relations, published in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, reviewed links between parent-child relationships and children's interactions with peers. It found that family experiences and children's relationships outside the home are connected, although this does not mean that one directly determines the other.The important distinction is that a cousin relationship can combine friendship, family expectations and comparison. Classmates may bring their own competitive pressures, but the emotional meaning of a cousin's success can be different when adults repeatedly compare the two children.What parents can do: Avoid turning cousins into benchmarks for achievement. Instead of saying, “Your cousin can do it, why can't you?”, acknowledge each child's progress separately. If children compete, help them learn to handle disappointment without making one child the winner in every family conversation.Children may use different social strategies in different groupsA child may be the one who organises every game with cousins but quietly follows a classmate's suggestions at school. Another may readily share snacks with friends but refuse to lend a toy to a cousin.Such differences can reflect the child's position within each group. Children may take on different roles depending on whom they are with, the group's established dynamics and what they think will help them belong.A review in the Annual Review of Psychology, Peer Relationships and Social Competence During Early and Middle Childhood, examines how children's peer acceptance, friendships and social competence develop. It highlights the importance of understanding children's relationships in context rather than treating social competence as a single, uniform quality.For instance, a child who is used to being the eldest among cousins may naturally take charge during play. At school, where several children have equally strong opinions, that same child may need to negotiate, take turns and compromise.The reverse is possible, too. A child who rarely gets to make decisions in a family group may feel more confident among classmates who appreciate their ideas.These differences can provide opportunities to practise cooperation, negotiation and flexibility. Parents need not insist that children behave identically in every setting, provided their behaviour remains respectful and safe.The relationship itself matters more than the labelIt is easy to assume that cousins are automatically closer because they are family. In reality, some children see their cousins every weekend, while others meet them only during holidays. Some share interests and ages; others have little in common.A child may feel safer with a classmate who listens without judging than with a cousin who teases them. Another child may prefer cousins because they have shared years of play and family experiences.A review of childhood friendships and peer networks emphasises that friendship quality, acceptance by a group and participation in peer networks are separate dimensions of children's social lives. Simply being part of a group does not guarantee that a child feels accepted or understood.This is why parents should look beyond the family-versus-school distinction. Ask whether the child feels included, whether disagreements are resolved fairly and whether they can express their preferences without fear of ridicule.If a child consistently dreads meeting certain cousins, becomes distressed before family gatherings or reports repeated teasing, adults should take those concerns seriously rather than dismissing them with “They're family, you should get along.”When should parents pay attention?Different behaviour across settings is not, by itself, a cause for concern. A child can be outgoing with familiar people and reserved in a classroom without there being anything wrong.Parents should pay closer attention when the change is intense, persistent or accompanied by signs of distress. For example, a child who regularly cries before meeting cousins, fears being mocked by classmates or feels compelled to change their behaviour to avoid rejection may need support.Rather than asking, “Why can't you behave the same way everywhere?”, try asking specific, open-ended questions:“What do you enjoy doing with your cousins?”“Is there anything that makes you uncomfortable when you play together?”“Do you feel you can say no when you don't want to play a game?”“Is there someone at school you feel especially comfortable with?”Listen without immediately correcting the child's account or insisting that they share everything with family. Their answers may help you understand whether the difference comes from familiarity, group dynamics, comparison or an uncomfortable relationship.If the distress is ongoing and affects the child's daily life, consider discussing it with a paediatrician or child mental health professional.The takeawayA child who behaves differently around cousins and classmates is not necessarily being inconsistent or putting on an act. Different relationships bring different expectations, histories and feelings of belonging. For parents, the goal is not to make a child equally talkative, confident or cooperative in every setting. It is to help them feel secure enough to express themselves, respect other people and navigate disagreements.Sometimes, the child who runs around the living room with cousins and stays quiet in class is simply responding to two very different social worlds. Understanding those worlds can tell parents far more than judging the behaviour alone.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: Dhruv Rathee flies to London and joins ‘Jantar Mantar’ protest
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from London: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee attended a protest outside the Mahatma Gandhi statue in London’s Parliament Square on Saturday over
articles.body: TOI correspondent from London: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee attended a protest outside the Mahatma Gandhi statue in London’s Parliament Square on Saturday over alleged irregularities in the special intensive revision of electoral rolls in India, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Despite calling Indians to attend the protest on his X handle, saying “It’s time the world sees the reality of vote chor and murderer of democracy,” Rathee, who flew to London from India on Friday, arrived at the protest on Saturday two hours late and then led chants and gave a speech. Hundreds of Indian students turned up waving Communist flags, Congress flags and Indian Workers Association flags. It was organised by SFI-UK and other groups. They chanted: “Modi is a traitor,” called for “Azadi” (freedom) from the current BJP govt and shouted “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod!” (“Vote thief, leave the throne”). Some held up a stuffed toy monkey.A smaller counter-protest was organised at the eleventh hour by pro-Modi supporters who waved the tricolour while shouting “Vande Mataram”, “Bharat Mata Ki Jai” and “Modi, Modi”. Hirdesh Gupta, who attended the counter-protest, said: “They are trying to make it an international issue and divide the Indian diaspora here which is very bad. This has got nothing to do with the UK.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Yet another infra scare, 12-tonne steel cage crashes onto moving car in Mumbai; MMRDA slaps Rs 2 crore fine
articles.summary: THANE: A massive 12-tonne steel reinforcement cage meant to form a pier of the under-construction Anand Nagar-Saket elevated road came crashing down on a
articles.body: THANE: A massive 12-tonne steel reinforcement cage meant to form a pier of the under-construction Anand Nagar-Saket elevated road came crashing down on a moving sedan on the busy Eastern Express Highway near Kopri railway bridge on Saturday afternoon, narrowly averting what could have been a major tragedy.The mishap occurred around 2pm on the Mumbai-bound carriageway. Eyewitnesses said they heard a loud creaking sound before the towering network of steel rods buckled and almost collapsed onto the passing car. The driver and his female passengers had a narrow escape even as the network of rods ripped open portion of the car roof and smashed the windshield."I initially thought some stone had fallen and immediately halted, but was shocked to see how narrowly we escaped. I suffered minor injuries to my head while my passenger also got minor injured but not requiring medical intervention," he told the media.The Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA), which is executing the project through a contractor, however claimed no injuries were reported. The Naupada police team that reached out to the driver said they refused to file a complaint. A station diary entry has been made, said an official.The incident has raised serious questions over construction safety on one of the city's busiest traffic corridors. With vehicles streaming through the stretch through the day, a similar collapse during peak-hour traffic could have had devastating consequences. Following the incident, the MMRDA announced a Rs 2-crore penalty on the contractor and ordered a detailed investigation into the collapse."We view this incident with utmost seriousness. Such incidents are unacceptable, and any lapse in construction safety will not be tolerated," the authority said in a statement, adding that corrective measures would be enforced to prevent a recurrence. articles.title: ‘Crocodiles will eat her’: How a shopping promise led to nursing officer’s murder
articles.summary: BHOPAL: A bridge over a river where crocodiles lurk may hold the key to the disappearance of a nursing officer whose body has not been found days after
articles.body: BHOPAL: A bridge over a river where crocodiles lurk may hold the key to the disappearance of a nursing officer whose body has not been found days after she went missing.Police suspect Snehlata, who hailed from Bihar, was strangled and thrown into the crocodile-infested waters of Pachnada in Uttar Pradesh’s Etawah district.The suspect allegedly told investigators that he believed crocodiles would consume her body, leaving little chance of recovering it.A confession leads police to the riverOn Thursday, police took the suspect, Satyaprakash, to Pachnada, the confluence of five rivers, around 60 km away, to search for the missing woman’s body.The operation was launched with assistance from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF).According to sources, Satyaprakash allegedly confessed during questioning that he strangled Snehlata and threw her body from a bridge into the river believing crocodiles would consume it.Police suspect crocodiles may have consumed her remains, but the body has not yet been recovered.A relationship, a child and mounting disputesSnehlata, who was from Bihar, met Satyaprakash, a resident of Joshi Nagar in Bhind, Madhya Pradesh, while studying at a private college where he worked. The two later entered a live-in relationship.Satyaprakash was already married. Snehlata gave birth to their son around 10 months ago. Police said disputes between the two intensified over the child and Snehlata’s demand that Satyaprakash recognise her as his wife.A shopping promise before she disappearedOn October 8, Satyaprakash allegedly took Snehlata away on the pretext of travelling to Kanpur, promising to take her shopping. She has not been seen since.He subsequently lodged a missing person report at Bhind City Kotwali police station and had flyers printed to help trace her. Police began questioning him after suspecting his role in her disappearance, following which he allegedly confessed to killing her.Family demands strict actionSnehlata’s family travelled from Nalanda in Bihar to Bhind after learning about the case. articles.title: In 1968, Cassandra Henderson graduated from a North Carolina school; nearly 60 years later, she moved back into the same building after it was restored from 20 years of vacancy into 53 senior apartments
articles.summary: Nearly six decades after graduating from Dillard Junior High School in Yanceyville, North Carolina, Cassandra Henderson has returned to the same building,
articles.body: Nearly six decades after graduating from Dillard Junior High School in Yanceyville, North Carolina, Cassandra Henderson has returned to the same building, this time as a resident of its newly restored senior apartments. The former school, which closed in 2002 and remained vacant for more than 20 years, has been transformed into 53 affordable homes for older adults. According to NC Newsline, which reported on the redevelopment, the project combines historic preservation with an effort to address the shortage of affordable housing for seniors. The development has also received national recognition from the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition.From school corridors to affordable homesHenderson graduated from the school in 1968 and later spent years living in Richmond, Virginia. When she wanted to return to Yanceyville to be closer to family and friends, finding suitable housing became an obstacle. Her sister encouraged her to move home, but Henderson recalled telling her there was nowhere for her to live. The redevelopment changed that. Henderson moved into the Dillard School Apartments in August 2026, returning to the entrance where she once arrived by school bus. In an interview with NC Newsline, she recalled the school’s hallways, metal lockers and auditorium, describing her years there as some of her happiest.She also expressed relief that the building had been preserved and given a new purpose. Her experience illustrates how converting an unused historic property into housing can help older residents remain connected to the communities where they grew up.A former school gets a second lifeThe building originally opened as the Caswell County Training School between 1949 and 1951. It was the first school in Caswell County to offer 11 grades to Black students. Following desegregation in 1969, it was renamed Dillard Junior High School in honour of Nicholas Longworth Dillard, a longtime principal.The school closed in 2002 and was subsequently listed on the National Register of Historic Places. However, it remained unused for more than two decades, with broken windows, a deteriorating gymnasium roof and interiors exposed to the elements.Alex Walker, a representative of the project's developer, DreamKey Partners, told NC Newsline that the conversion offered an opportunity to preserve the historic building while putting it back into productive use. Rather than demolishing the property, the redevelopment retained its historic character and adapted the former educational spaces for residential use.What the 53 apartments offerThe completed Dillard School Senior Apartments development contains 53 affordable homes for residents aged 62 and older. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, the property comprises seven studio apartments and 46 one-bedroom units, with rents restricted to households earning no more than 50% of the area median income. Residents pay up to 30% of their income towards rent, with federal housing assistance covering the remaining eligible costs. The development is intended for older adults who can live independently rather than those requiring assisted-living services.The property also includes elevators, accessible features, a community centre with computer and fitness facilities, communal laundry, tenant storage and community gardens. Outdoor amenities include pickleball and shuffleboard courts, while on-site management helps coordinate services for residents.These facilities are intended to make the apartments practical for older adults while providing opportunities for recreation and social interaction.Addressing North Carolina's senior housing shortageThe redevelopment comes as affordable housing remains difficult to find for many older North Carolinians living on fixed incomes. According to figures cited by NC Newsline, approximately 42% of renters and 20% of homeowners in Caswell County spend more than 30% of their gross monthly income on housing. Across North Carolina, the estimated shortage of affordable rental homes for extremely low-income households stands at 215,000.Charity James, property manager at Dillard School Apartments, told NC Newsline that the community has few affordable housing developments, particularly those designed for seniors. She said demand exceeded the number of available apartments when leasing began, resulting in long waiting lists. The project cannot resolve the wider housing shortage on its own, but it provides an example of how unused public-serving buildings can be adapted to meet local housing needs.How the restoration was financedThe project combined several funding sources, including the US Department of Housing and Urban Development's Section 202 programme and state and federal historic tax credits. Walker told NC Newsline that combining these financing mechanisms, particularly HUD support, made it possible to restore the property and provide affordable homes. The development received the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition's 2026 Recognition of Housing Tax Credit Excellence award in the rural housing category. Emily Cadik, the coalition's chief executive, said the winning projects had made lasting contributions to their communities by providing families with affordable places to live.For Henderson, however, the redevelopment's importance is personal. She has returned not simply to her hometown but to a building that holds memories of her school years. In an interview with NC Newsline, she described being back as a source of renewed energy and said she felt she was where she belonged. The former school now serves a different generation, preserving a piece of local history while giving older residents an opportunity to remain close to home.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kolkata stampede: Video shows crowd breaching barricades, tussling with cops at Chorbagan pandal day before tragedy
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Videos showing revellers pushing past barricades and tussling with police personnel at north Kolkata’s Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal has brought
articles.body: KOLKATA: Videos showing revellers pushing past barricades and tussling with police personnel at north Kolkata’s Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal has brought into focus the mounting crowd pressure at the venue in the days leading up to Saturday’s stampede, which claimed 19 lives and left 25 people injured.The pandal, one of the city’s biggest crowd-pullers this year, had witnessed heavy footfall since opening, with temporary restrictions on crowd movement imposed on multiple occasions over the preceding four days to stagger the rush.Despite these measures, the arrangements proved inadequate to handle the pressure, according to accounts from the area.Located inside the narrow Radha Madhab Saha Lane, the pandal was among the three adjudged ‘Serar-sera’ by the state government this year. Its popularity drew large numbers of visitors, with crowds spilling out onto Central Avenue and thousands waiting in the narrow approach lane to enter.The location had long been a concern for authorities, given the limited space available to regulate entry and exit and the difficulty of dispersing large crowds once the lane became congested.Rain triggers surge as visitors crowd inside pandalThe situation turned tragic around 7.30pm on Saturday, the first of the two Saptami days on the 2026 puja calendar, when a sudden spell of rain prompted visitors to rush inside the pandal for shelter. What began as a drizzle soon turned into a torrential downpour, which lasted nearly an hour.With people reluctant to step out into the rain, those gathered near the entrance continued to push forward, adding to the pressure on visitors already inside.Eyewitnesses said thousands were waiting in the queue when the skies opened up. Those who had completed their visit were unable to move out because people ahead were refusing to leave the shelter of the pandal.As the pressure from behind increased, the crowd became difficult to control. One eyewitness recalled feeling a huge push before stumbling forward, with several people falling near a flight of stairs close to the exit. Others fell over them as the crush intensified, while some visitors managed to escape and others had to be pulled out after local residents dismantled a portion of the pandal.A first-person account by Ram Sarkar, whose wife Arati died in the stampede, described how the situation deteriorated within minutes. Sarkar said he had initially suggested skipping Chorbagan because he expected it to be crowded, but his wife insisted on visiting after seeing videos of the pandal’s interiors on social media. By the time they arrived, the area was packed, and the queue had spilled onto Central Avenue.Sarkar said the crowd began rushing towards the pandal as the rain intensified. According to his account, volunteers removed barricades and allowed people to enter, apparently fearing that visitors might leave.Inside, he said, it was dark and packed, leaving little room to breathe. When people began pushing from behind, he fell and became separated from his wife.He recalled people shouting and screaming as he struggled to get back on his feet. Once he managed to stand, he began searching frantically for Arati. He saw people lying on the ground and relatives crying for help, but alleged that no volunteers, police personnel or organisers came forward to assist them.He eventually found his wife lying motionless and called for help, but said no ambulance was immediately available. It took more than an hour to arrange one, he said. Doctors later told him that Arati had died.Narrow exits, crowd management under scannerOther eyewitnesses and local residents also alleged that crowd-management arrangements at the pandal were inadequate. Several questioned whether enough police personnel and volunteers had been deployed to handle the rush, with some claiming that police presence was concentrated near the VIP entrance.Questions were also raised over announcements about entry, exit and crowd movement, which visitors said had left people confused during the rush.The pandal’s layout is also being examined as part of the investigation. The design required visitors to descend a flight of stairs from an upper deck to the lower level near the exit, a feature believed to have contributed to the difficulties in moving people out during the surge. Sources said a change in the puja committee had also meant that people with previous experience in crowd management were no longer in charge.The sudden downpour added another layer of difficulty. Although the Met office had forecast sporadic rain, the evening spell was sharper and more prolonged than expected. H R Biswas, deputy director general of meteorology, said the showers were linked to the retreating monsoon. A weather official said the rain had made the ground soggy and affected people’s footing, while its persistence for more than 45 minutes contributed to the conditions in which the crowd surge unfolded.The stampede left families scrambling to locate relatives as victims were rushed to Calcutta Medical College and Hospital from around 8pm. The emergency department was overwhelmed as injured people continued to arrive until late in the evening.Police restricted access to parts of the hospital, leaving anxious relatives struggling to obtain information about their loved ones. Some family members alleged that victims had been brought in private cars and cabs because emergency arrangements were inadequate.Among those who died was 18-year-old Tania, who had gone pandal-hopping with friends. Her mother, Rupa Biswas, said she received a call around 8.30pm informing her that Tania was at the hospital and had been declared dead. Tania’s friends told her that several people had fallen on top of the teenager during the stampede. Suman Sonkar, 21, was another victim. Her sister, Shreya, alleged that people were lying around after the incident but that there were no volunteers or organisers to help transport them to hospital.Priya Samaddar, 20, from Madhyamgram, had also gone pandal-hopping with a friend. Her father, Shyamal Samaddar, said he rushed to the hospital after receiving news of her death but was not allowed to see his daughter immediately. Other families continued searching for relatives whose whereabouts remained unknown, while some questioned who would be held responsible for the deaths.14 detained; major pujas shut as safety measures reviewedPolice have detained 14 people, including organisers of the Chorbagan Durga Puja, for questioning. Investigators are examining CCTV footage collected from the area and speaking to the puja committee, police personnel and those employed to manage the crowd.The list of security guards and other staff deployed at the venue has also been sought. A forensic team reached the pandal late on Saturday night to collect evidence.Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari visited the hospital and met families of the deceased. He said an initial assessment suggested that an announcement made by the puja committee may have contributed to the incident. The state government has announced compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a government job for the next of kin of each person who died, along with Rs 5 lakh for each injured person. The chief minister said the incident would be investigated and action taken against those found responsible.Adhikari also urged puja organisers to follow safety guidelines and ensure adequate illumination inside pandals, warning against theme-based installations that remain dimly lit. He said the investigation would examine whether organisers, homeguards, temporary workers, police personnel or private security guards had failed in their duties. The administration has also begun reviewing crowd-management arrangements at other major pujas.Within hours of the Chorbagan tragedy, several prominent Durga Puja organisers across Kolkata were asked to temporarily stop admitting visitors. Tala Pratyay, Alipore Sarbojanin, Chetla Agrani and Ballygunge Sarbojonin were among the crowd-pullers asked to suspend entry, while the show at Allen Park was cancelled. Santosh Mitra Square reduced the number of visitors allowed inside, and major pujas in Salt Lake were also asked to stop entry as a precaution.At Chetla Agrani in south Kolkata, organisers said they had acted to prevent another tragedy after a sudden spell of rain led to a sharp increase in the crowd inside the pandal. Volunteers raised concerns about the pressure, following which police assessed the situation and ordered an evacuation. The organisers closed the entry gates, opened the exits and removed barricades to allow people to disperse. They said the situation had not reached the point of a stampede.Chetla Agrani had also been shut down temporarily the previous year after a spark caused by a short circuit was spotted and extinguished. This time, its organisers said, they had complied with the police order as soon as concerns emerged. Tala Pratyay also stopped entry and said it would reassess illumination, entry and exit points, and crowd-management arrangements before reopening. Allen Park stopped its music and laser show, while Santosh Mitra Square said it had widened entry and exit points and was working to limit the number of visitors inside.Other organisers said they were monitoring crowd movement and increasing the number of volunteers. Suruchi Sangha in Chetla said visitors were being asked to keep moving rather than congregate in front of the idol. Authorities were expected to review arrangements with organisers before deciding when the major pandals could reopen.The incident has revived concerns over crowd management at Kolkata’s biggest Durga Puja attractions, where elaborate themes and social media visibility draw thousands of visitors into limited spaces. The Chorbagan pandal’s narrow approach lane, the queue extending onto a major road, the reported removal of barricades, the rain-driven rush for shelter and the difficulties faced by people trying to exit are among the circumstances investigators are examining.The last major stampede-like incident during Durga Puja in Kolkata was at Deshapriya Park in 2015, when an 88-foot Durga idol billed as the world’s tallest drew enormous crowds and paralysed traffic across large parts of south Kolkata. Several people fell ill and sustained injuries amid the rush, but there were no deaths. The Chorbagan tragedy, by contrast, has left 19 families mourning relatives who had stepped out to celebrate the festival.As the city’s festive music gave way to ambulance sirens and emergency announcements on Saturday night, many revellers abandoned their plans and headed home. articles.title: 'Kicked me for 10 minutes': Trump 'disturbed' by images of attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine by Israeli settlers
articles.summary: The attack by Israeli settlers on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine in the West Bank has drawn widespread condemnation, with US Secretary of
articles.body: The attack by Israeli settlers on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine in the West Bank has drawn widespread condemnation, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying President Donald Trump was disturbed by the images of the incident."We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing, the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank," Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews.US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called for action against those responsible and said Washington had demanded a full investigation into the incident."Heidi Levine, photojournalist for Washington Post suffered serious injuries from vicious & cowardly attack. Heidi is US Citizen, clear ID as journalist. Details of who under investigation, but those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison. We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this. Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonourable act of senseless violence," he said.Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine underwent surgery at Beilinson Hospital on Saturday after being attacked by Jewish rioters during an olive harvest in the Binyamin region of the West Bank on Friday.The Jerusalem Post reported that Levine's condition was moderate and that she had sustained injuries to her limbs.Speaking to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) from her hospital bed, Levine said she was “attacked by a gang of masked settlers”.“They pushed me to the ground and they were kicking me for, I think at least 10 minutes,” she said, adding that she had identified herself as an American journalist.“Hopefully nothing is broken, but I will need stitches in my hand, stitches on my back,” she added.Levine said she did not personally see Israeli military personnel at the scene but saw tear gas and stun grenades being fired, suggesting that Israeli soldiers may have been present. She also said her bag, camera and phone were stolen during the attack.In a separate incident on Saturday, Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, Palestinian olive harvesters and a visiting French mayor in the occupied West Bank. Vehicles belonging to diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland were targeted in the Taybeh area.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later said there was a lack of “compelling evidence” regarding the attack on the European diplomats, appearing to suggest that the incident was part of a “coordinated smear campaign”.Settler violence has drawn increasing international criticism as Israel continues to expand settlements in the West Bank, which it captured in 1967. Around 500,000 Israelis live in the territory alongside approximately three million Palestinians. Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law.Despite repeated condemnations by Israeli officials and calls from foreign governments for accountability, prosecutions of settlers accused of violent crimes against Palestinians remain rare.You use AI every day. articles.title: Julia Roberts’ 51-acre New Mexico ranch hosted her 2002 wedding to Danny Moder, with Brad Pitt and George Clooney among 50 Hollywood guests
articles.summary: Julia Roberts’ former Taos ranch holds a place in Hollywood history as the setting for her 2002 wedding to cinematographer Danny Moder.
articles.body: Julia Roberts’ former Taos ranch holds a place in Hollywood history as the setting for her 2002 wedding to cinematographer Danny Moder. The 51-acre New Mexico property, with its canyon views and secluded surroundings, offered a private setting for the actress to celebrate away from the usual public attention. Their midnight ceremony on 4 July brought around 50 guests to the ranch, including George Clooney and Brad Pitt. A small wooden chapel, a white reception tent and a relaxed Western-inspired dress code shaped the occasion, turning Roberts’ private retreat into the backdrop for one of the most talked-about moments in her personal life.Julia Roberts’ 51-acre New Mexico ranch offered a private wedding settingRoberts’ ranch covered 51 acres in the Taos area, providing room for a celebration away from the attention that ordinarily followed the actress. The property had a canyon view and enough space for the couple to hold their wedding outdoors, with a temporary white tent erected for guests. Roberts had also built a small wooden chapel on the land, adding a more permanent feature to a place that served as her private home and retreat.Taos, in northern New Mexico, has long attracted people looking for a quieter setting among high desert terrain, mountains and expansive skies. For Roberts, the ranch offered a degree of privacy that would have been difficult to find at a conventional wedding venue. Its appeal was not simply the scenery. The event could be arranged on familiar ground, with guests brought in for a private gathering rather than a public-facing ceremony.Julia Roberts’ 2002 wedding featured 50 guests and a rain-soaked ceremonyAs reported by The New York Post, Roberts married Moder in the early hours of 4 July 2002, at a ceremony that began around midnight. The date gave the gathering an Independence Day connection, while the invitations set out a deliberately informal mix of summer garden party and Western-inspired style. Guests were encouraged to wear light fabrics and summer hats rather than formal black-tie clothing.Around 50 guests attended, according to the New York Post report published the following day. Among them were George Clooney and Brad Pitt, both familiar figures in Roberts’ professional circle, as well as director Steven Soderbergh, who had worked with her on Ocean’s Eleven and Erin Brockovich. The guest list was small by celebrity-event standards, but it included people whose presence gave the private occasion a distinctly Hollywood dimension.Weather briefly threatened to become an unwelcome part of the proceedings. Heavy rain and thunderstorms had swept through the area during the preceding afternoon, leaving the ground wet and the skies unsettled. The downpour eased about half an hour after the ceremony began, allowing the celebration to continue.A bohemian dress code and cowboy hats shaped the ranch weddingThe wedding’s dress code reflected the couple’s choice of setting. Their invitation combined references to Shakespearean midsummer festivities with the glamour associated with The Great Gatsby and a bohemian interpretation of the American West. Guests were asked to dress for warm weather and an outdoor party, with linen and seersucker among the suggested fabrics.Cowboy hats appeared among the guests, fitting the ranch surroundings without turning the occasion into a formal Western-themed production. A spacious white tent provided shelter and space for the gathering, while the celebration carried on beyond sunrise. Food included Southwestern-style barbecue, according to the contemporary report.The arrangements were informal in appearance, but the guest list and location ensured that the wedding attracted attention. Journalists and photographers gathered outside the estate, attempting to catch a glimpse of the proceedings from beyond the property's boundaries. The ranch's privacy could limit access, even if it could not prevent public interest in Roberts’ marriage.How Roberts and Moder came togetherRoberts and Moder met while working on The Mexican, the 2001 film starring Roberts and Pitt. Moder was working as a cinematographer, and their professional connection developed into a relationship that eventually led to the New Mexico wedding. At the time, Moder was still married to makeup artist Vera Steimberg, from whom he later separated. Their relationship drew considerable tabloid attention in the period before the wedding.For Roberts, the marriage came after several highly publicised relationships. She had previously married country singer Lyle Lovett in 1993; the marriage ended after less than two years. Her personal life had attracted press coverage since the success of Pretty woman in 1990, and her relationships were often treated as part of the wider celebrity narrative surrounding her career.The wedding to Moder marked a new chapter, though the couple kept the details of the ceremony largely private. Roberts’ publicist confirmed the marriage after the event, while the precise arrangements remained limited to what guests and contemporary reports revealed.Disclaimer: This article is based on information available online. articles.title: A California farm earned about $100 per acre a year from dry-farmed wheat; after Alan Changala leased 300 acres for solar at $1,000 per acre, the same land began paying roughly 10 times the crop income
articles.summary: On the Changala family farm in Tulare County, California, a dirt road and a barbed-wire fence separate two very different ways of using the same land.
articles.body: On the Changala family farm in Tulare County, California, a dirt road and a barbed-wire fence separate two very different ways of using the same land. On one side, wheat grows with little irrigation. On the other, rows of solar panels turn sunlight into electricity for thousands of Southern California homes. For Alan Changala, the choice was not sentimental. The solar lease paid about ten times what the dry-farmed wheat could earn.Changala leased 300 acres of his father’s 1,400-acre farm to solar developers at $1,000 per acre, while the wheat operation generated roughly $100 per acre annually, reported The Sacramento Bee. The deal, negotiated at the family kitchen table in 2014, became part of a wider shift across California’s San Joaquin Valley, where farmers facing water shortages and rising costs are looking to solar as a way to keep their businesses viable. Read more about it here, as reported by The Sacramento Bee:Dry farming left little marginThe Changala farm had water available from wells and an irrigation canal, but using it was expensive. Instead, Alan Changala said nearly the entire property was dry-farmed, relying on rainfall rather than irrigation. That approach allowed wheat to be planted on about half the farm every other year, using a rotation system that preserved soil moisture.The economics were modest. Changala told The Sacramento Bee that the wheat business worked out to an annual income of about $100 per acre. In a region where water has become both scarce and costly, that limited return made it difficult to justify expanding irrigation or relying entirely on traditional crops.When solar developers began showing interest in the property, Changala saw an opportunity rather than a betrayal of his farming roots. He described himself as “a farmer, through and through,” but acknowledged that the lease was simply more profitable than continuing to farm every acre.Solar became the better cropThe lease covered 300 acres and paid $1,000 per acre, giving the family an income roughly ten times higher than the wheat operation. Changala said the arrangement did not take much persuasion, even though he negotiated carefully. Hal Dittmer of Sacramento renewable-energy developer Wellhead Electric personally negotiated the deal with the Changala family in 2014, as per the report.Construction took place in 2015 and 2016. The completed project, technically made up of two facilities called Nicolis and Tropico, has a generating capacity of 34 megawatts and produces enough electricity to power about 9,000 homes in Southern California Edison’s service area. But Changala’s father, Si Changala, was less comfortable with the change. Still, he accepted the reality of the decision, saying farmers had to “go with the times.”Water shortages changed the mathThe shift toward solar is closely tied to California’s water crisis. The state’s Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, known as SGMA, requires farmers to gradually reduce groundwater pumping in areas where aquifers have been depleted by decades of overuse. In the San Joaquin Valley, that could mean retiring large amounts of farmland over the next two decades.The Public Policy Institute of California predicted that at least 535,000 acres of Valley farmland could be permanently retired over 20 years as farmers cut water use. The institute also estimated that about 50,000 of those idled acres could be converted to solar farms.For farmers like Changala, solar offers a way to earn steady income from land that may no longer be practical to farm. He was even negotiating to lease another 400 acres for a second solar facility, a move that would further reduce the footprint of the family’s wheat operation.Solar brings income but few jobsThe financial benefits for individual landowners are clear, but the broader economic effects are more complicated. Solar farms create substantial employment during construction, but once the panels are operating, they require relatively few permanent workers. On the Changala property, workers arrived in school buses during installation, but the completed site now depends mainly on occasional maintenance visits and remote operations based in Southern California.Local officials worry that this lack of permanent employment weakens the economic base of rural communities. In Kern County, where thousands of acres have already been converted to solar, planning director Lorelei Oviatt said land removed from farming “doesn’t pay for libraries,” pointing to the county’s need for jobs, services and quality of life for its 900,000 residents.There are also concerns about tax revenue. California allowed solar project owners to avoid property taxes on the value of installed panels, meaning many facilities were taxed as though the land remained agricultural. Critics said the break, which was set to run until 2025, shifted costs away from a mature industry and onto counties.A difficult trade-off for the ValleyCalifornia still needs solar power. Utilities in the state received one-third of their electricity from renewable sources at the time, and state law required that share to rise to 60 percent by 2030 and 100 percent by 2045. The San Joaquin Valley, with its abundant sunlight and large tracts of land, could play a major role in meeting those targets.But converting farmland to solar is not a simple solution. Community leaders worry about unplanned patches of retired land, dust, weeds and air-quality problems. Some farm groups are working with environmental organisations to create conservation easements that would pay farmers to restore land as wildlife habitat rather than leave it idle or cover it with panels.For the Changala family, however, the decision came down to survival. Wheat still grows on one side of the fence, but solar panels now provide a far stronger financial foundation on the other. As Alan Changala put it, “We’re still farming the sun.”You use AI every day.
